title: Economy and Resources
summary: Maps currencies, sources, sinks, materials and economic guardrails so progression remains understandable and sustainable.

blocks.text: The economy of Symphony of Justice must clearly distinguish among:
Currencies → Progression Resources → Materials → Equipment → Temporary Resources
Not every item accumulated by the player should become a "currency."
The proposed core economy is as follows:

The original documents already distinguish materials for characters, weapons, and talents, as well as regional resources, dishes, recipes, and materials. They also define Last Wills as harder-to-obtain equipment tied to weekly bosses and Dungeons, capable of working in smaller one- or two-piece sets.
The provisional narrative name remains: TBD
This is the main economic currency used in gameplay.

There should not be a different common currency for each nation.
Regions may have their own materials, but fragmenting the basic currency by territory would add complexity without improving gameplay.

The historical documentation provisionally calls it Service Currency. Its value can be exchanged for the game's Premium Currency, and it is also associated with a daily login benefit. It can also be earned through daily in-game activities as part of the daily login system.
I propose keeping the concept, although not necessarily the name.
The historical documentation provisionally calls it Interactive Currency, obtained with real money and also tied to a monthly login benefit.
I propose keeping the concept, although not necessarily the name.
It must always be displayed separately from free currency.
This resource is directly associated with the Gacha system.
It may be obtained for free or by converting Premium Currency.
The system does not need three or more different types of tickets unless a clear design reason emerges later.

There are only two types of Tickets. The first is tied to limited-time Banners, which change with each cycle or version. The other is tied to the Permanent Banner, which does not change and has fixed benefits.

Once the maximum is reached, the player receives the corresponding rewards: Service Currency (name still TBD).
Every permanent currency or resource must have a clear source within gameplay.
Play → earn → decide where to invest.
It should be the most common currency.
It does not need a low possession cap.

This currency should allow the player to adapt and obtain Tickets or other high-value items.
It does not need a possession cap, since players may save it or invest it in whichever Tickets they prefer.
It should be sufficient for a free-to-play player to participate in the Gacha system regularly, although the final rate requires economic simulation.
The historical documentation specifically includes a currency purchased with real money and a monthly benefit tied to it.
It should not be farmable in meaningful quantities as Premium Currency, because that would eliminate the clear economic distinction between the two layers.
It even proposes that Blacksmithing may produce selected experience resources.
Exploration is already intended to be the main way to obtain ascension materials and enemy drops.

The documentation already includes specific enemies associated with Illumination, Darkness, Spectrum, Seals, and the natural elements. However, as their versions are updated and the world expands, these Bosses and items may be expanded or changed. Some may stop being obtainable, or certain characters may use materials from another Boss tied to their Nation or environment.
This comes directly from the original design.
Their drop frequency should be lower than that of conventional artifacts.

Alchemy is designed to craft consumables related to exploration, chests, regional materials, talent books, and refinement. Cooking produces food that can modify stats, restore health, and even provide effects tied to the identity of specific characters.
A Sink is any system that permanently removes resources from the economy.
Without enough Sinks, the pattern becomes: Play → accumulate → stop needing rewards.
At that point, a major part of the Core Loop loses its value.
They should not be fully recoverable after use.
The project already has a particularly useful Sink:
The documentation proposes sacrificing artifacts of the same set, piece, and rarity to increase the probability of obtaining desired attributes.

For that reason, the mechanism can become one of the main Endgame Sinks.

This prevents purposeless accumulation of Banner residue indefinitely.
It must be spent during the event itself.
When the event ends, it may:
remain available in the shop during a grace period until it is spent, or expire unused if the player does not have enough to purchase anything.
I would not use taxes or automatic loss of permanent resources.
The economy should encourage spending, not punish saving.
The overall economy can be represented through several loops.
The importance of these three complementary activities is already established in the parent document.
This loop is especially effective because it turns a poor reward into potential progress.
Premium Currency enters as an alternative route to Tickets, not as their exclusive source.
Dead or redundant loops to avoid
"Cooking Currency," "Blacksmithing Currency," "Alchemy Currency," "Cryo Currency," and so on.
Daily points must disappear at the end of the daily cycle because they measure progress; they are not stored wealth.
We may have materials with different rarities, but we do not need five completely independent experience systems.
Before introducing a new resource, we must answer:

Where is it obtained?
Where is it spent?
If either answer is missing, the resource is not ready yet.
Regions should have distinctive materials, but they should not reproduce exactly the same currency with a different icon.
Farming must exist because Symphony of Justice has characters, weapons, builds, and crafting systems that require progression.
However, the historical document itself states that daily quests should not become trivial and boring activities, and it proposes a system of varied Hunts with different point values.
I propose that basic exploration and normal enemies should not use a universal energy system.

The premium economy must remain separate from the economy required to complete the game.
What can be purchased with real money
The documentation already includes outfits and housing decorations as commercial products.
This is a particularly healthy premium Sink because:
However, they must never contain mandatory exclusive power.

The old document proposed purchasing a pass that increased the maximum number of Dungeon rewards. This is one of the main objectives, unlike battle passes that have both a free track and a premium track.

This pass extends or expands the monthly limit. For example, the standard pass may accumulate up to 1,000 points, while the extended pass raises the limit to 2,500, allowing the player to keep playing freely with friends and earning rewards.

This distinction matters: the player is not prevented from playing again or repeating the loop with friends. What is limited is the earning of special items, such as Service Currency and time-gated materials, which the pass expands.
A cleaner alternative would be a membership or pass system that grants additional rewards.
The documentation also includes the option to purchase resources.
competitive power that is impossible to obtain through gameplay.
Therefore, paying increases purchasing capacity, but it does not create exclusive access to the system.
Inflation occurs when the player obtains resources much faster than they can use them. In a live-service RPG, this can cause two opposite problems:
The player has millions of resources with no value.
Each new upgrade requires so many layers of resources that developing a character turns into a fantasy tax audit.
We need to remain between these two extremes.
Characters, weapons, talents, crafting, and builds.
Not everything can be solved by accumulating money alone.
This preserves the value of playing content.
Conceptual example: 3 lower-tier materials → 1 higher-tier material.
An excellent Sink for surplus equipment.
They prevent a player from accumulating ten years of currency and instantly buying out every future shop.
7. New Sinks, not simply enormous costs
When the economy accumulates surpluses, it is preferable to introduce:
instead of simply multiplying a skill's cost by ten.
During Alpha/Beta, we should measure at least:
How much Common Currency a player obtains per:
How much the player spends during the same periods.
If 80% of players hold enormous quantities of a resource, its Sink is insufficient.
If almost no one has any, the resource is probably too restricted.
How many minutes per week the player needs to maintain their team.
What percentage of resources comes from:
If nearly everything comes from a single activity, the economy is constricting the Core Loop.
The historical points system makes it possible to measure this behavior precisely.
This will be essential for validating the Sacrifice Mechanism.
How many free Wishes a player earns per version.
This is not intended to design artificial difficulty, but to understand commercial sustainability.
Identify which resource most often blocks progress:
a character ready + a weapon ready + zero talent books for four weeks
would be a sign of an unbalanced economy.
If players quit after facing specific farming requirements, that resource deserves investigation.
